strengths: Targets an important and under-explored setting: panoramic semantic occupancy prediction for legged/humanoid robots under gait jitter, 360° coverage, and tight compute/payload constraints.
Proposes a complete vision-only pipeline (DP-ER, BGV, GDC, AMoE-3D) and validates via ablations that each component adds to final mIoU on QuadOcc.

Introduces two benchmarks: QuadOcc (real quadruped 360° with 10 scenes/24K frames/6 classes) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego 360° with 160 sequences/8K frames, depth, pose, multiple splits), which could be useful community resources.

Achieves strong empirical results: 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc, surpassing LMSCNet (18.44) and MonoScene (19.19) with only a panoramic camera; on Human360Occ gains +3.83 mIoU within-city and +8.08 mIoU cross-city over the best vision baseline.
Reports day/dusk/night robustness and qualitative comparisons showing better global layout, 360° continuity, and occlusion handling than baselines.
Provides efficiency measurements (101.76M parameters, 14.3 FPS on RTX4090) and an extrapolated Jetson Thor estimate, supporting the lightweight motivation.
Paper is generally clear, with informative figures and a well-motivated problem statement.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is mostly integrative: dual-projection fusion, bi-grid voxelization, mixture-of-experts decoding, and displacement compensation are adapted from existing ideas; no new theoretical formulation is presented.

The paper does not compare against recent panoramic/omnidirectional SSC methods such as OmniOcc or OccCylindrical, despite citing them, so the claimed state-of-the-art is only relative to the selected baselines.

GDC lacks direct validation: no evidence is provided that the learned displacements correspond to gait-induced camera motion; it may learn dataset-specific offsets, and single-frame inference cannot disambiguate ego-motion from object motion.

Evaluation is limited to validation splits on two datasets (one real, one simulated) with no held-out test set, no real humanoid/legged deployment, and no measured embedded latency; the Jetson Thor estimate is extrapolated rather than measured.

The benchmarks and code are only promised, not released, and the main paper omits key implementation details (e.g., BGV per-voxel convex weights, AMoE-3D expert count/gating, baseline training/config specifics), limiting reproducibility.

Ablations are only on QuadOcc; there is no component analysis on Human360Occ or cross-city robustness, and the QuadOcc gain over MonoScene is modest (+1.37 mIoU). Night mIoU trails MonoScene (13.50 vs 14.20).
Baseline fairness is not fully established: some baselines use extra modalities (P+D, P+L) or are retrained with 'minimal changes' without statistical significance or error bars.
The temporal-coherence motivation is not fully addressed: the method is single-frame and does not use temporal fusion to correct gait jitter over time.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored yet practically important problem: semantic occupancy prediction for legged/humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera, explicitly targeting gait-induced jitter and 360° continuity that forward-facing wheeled-platform SSC pipelines do not handle.

Introduces two new benchmarks (QuadOcc, a real quadruped 360° dataset, and Human360Occ/H30, a CARLA human-ego 360° dataset with RGB, depth, and occupancy), which fill a genuine gap and are likely to be useful to the community beyond this paper.

The method is well-motivated and coherent: Dual-Projection fusion (DP-ER), Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV), Hierarchical AMoE-3D decoder, and Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) are each justified with clear reasoning tied to the panoramic/legged setting, and the zero-init GDC head is a sensible design choice.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: OneOcc reaches 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc (surpassing LMSCNet 18.44 and MonoScene 19.19) and 37.29/32.23 mIoU on H30 within-/cross-city, with the cross-city gain (+8.08) supporting a robustness claim. Ablations (Table 4) show additive gains for each component.
Lightweight and efficient (101.76M params, ~14–19 FPS on RTX 4090 with mixed precision), with an onboard-deployment extrapolation to Jetson Thor, which is appropriate for the stated robotics target.
Clear writing, thorough related work, and good qualitative comparisons (Fig. 4) that illustrate suppression of frustum artifacts and improved 360° layout continuity.
weaknesses: Individual components are largely adaptations of existing ideas (dual projection, polar/cylindrical voxelization, MoE decoders, displacement/flow compensation); the novelty lies mainly in their combination for the panoramic-legged setting rather than in fundamentally new mechanisms.

QuadOcc ground truth is semi-automatic (multi-frame LiDAR aggregation, Grounded-SAM initialization, targeted manual fixes); the quality and consistency of this GT, and its potential impact on the reported metrics, is not quantitatively analyzed (e.g., no GT noise/ablation study or inter-annotator-style sanity check).

Dataset scale is modest (24K frames for QuadOcc, 8K for H30), and Human360Occ is simulated, so evidence for real-world humanoid deployment remains limited; the H30 gains may partly reflect simulation-specific statistics.

The 'rivaling/surpassing LiDAR' claim needs qualification: LiDAR baselines are re-trained/adapted on the new benchmarks and input modalities differ, so the comparison conflates sensor modality with pipeline design. A fairer framing would separate these factors.
GDC explicitly assumes accurate calibration with bounded drift; robustness to realistic calibration error or extrinsics drift is assumed rather than evaluated, despite being flagged as a limitation.

The public dataset/code URL in the abstract appears truncated, and reproducibility details (e.g., exact splits, annotation protocol for the manual fixes) are summarized rather than fully specified in the provided text.

strengths: Targets a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant setting: camera-only panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid platforms, with a well-articulated motivation (360° coverage, strict payload/power budgets, gait-induced body motion) that is distinct from the dominant forward-facing, wheeled-vehicle SSC literature.

Releases two benchmarks that fill a real data gap for this subarea: QuadOcc (real quadruped, 10 scenes / 24K frames, day/dusk/night, 6 classes) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego, 160 sequences / 8K frames, 16 maps, within-city and cross-city splits). A standardized panoramic SSC benchmark is a useful community contribution even if the method itself is not groundbreaking.

Results are consistent and positive across both benchmarks (20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc vs 19.19 MonoScene and 18.44 LMSCNet; 37.29/32.23 mIoU on H3O-Homo/Heter, i.e. +3.83/+8.08 over MonoScene), and Table 4 shows an additive ablation in which every proposed module yields a positive delta (+0.39, +0.31, +0.41, +0.26).
Reports deployment-relevant efficiency numbers (69.93 ms, ~14.3 FPS, 101.76M params, 1.86 GB peak on RTX 4090), which are appropriate for the stated embedded target.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, the pipeline figure is readable, and the problem formulation and loss choices are described concretely enough to follow.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional rather than conceptual. Dual-projection (raw annulus + equirectangular), hybrid Cartesian/polar voxelization, MoE/attention 3D fusion, and a learned 2D sampling-offset head are all established ingredients (cf. Cylinder3D, PointOcc, OccCylindrical, OmniOcc). 'Hierarchical AMoE-3D' is a depthwise-separable 3D UNet with channel/spatial gates and MoE Conv experts; the paper does not isolate a fundamentally new mechanism, only a re-combination tuned for a new platform.

The central claim — robustness to gait-induced jitter — is never directly validated. There is no experiment that injects, measures, or sweeps jitter magnitude, no analysis correlating the learned displacement Δs with actual robot motion, and no test on motion-corrupted sequences. GDC's benefit is inferred solely from a +0.39 mIoU ablation. On Human360Occ the gait is simulated in CARLA, so the motivating phenomenon is not established for real legged platforms at all; the paper's headline framing rests on an unmeasured effect.

Comparison scope is too narrow for the SOTA claim. Directly related panoramic/omnidirectional SSC methods that the paper itself cites (OmniOcc [69], GenOcc [70], OccCylindrical [71], the panoramic SSC survey [36]) are not compared against. Most baselines are older methods (SSCNet 2017, LMSCNet 2020, MonoScene 2022), and adapting perspective-camera models via unwrapping plausibly handicaps them near the poles, so the margin over 'best vision baseline' is not cleanly attributable to the proposed design.

Geometry vs. semantics trade-off is not addressed. On QuadOcc, OneOcc has the best mIoU (20.56) but its geometric IoU (48.92) is clearly below LMSCNet (55.40) and essentially on par with MonoScene (48.69). For a robotics application where occupancy geometry drives footstep planning, the paper should discuss why semantic mIoU improves while geometric fidelity regresses, but it reports only the favorable metric.

The new benchmark's ground truth is not analyzed. QuadOcc labels are produced by multi-frame LiDAR aggregation + Grounded-SAM initialization + 'targeted manual fixes' with no annotation-quality study, agreement measurement, or sanity check reported. Because the benchmark is the paper's principal asset, the absence of any GT validation is a material gap. The resolution is also very coarse (0.4 m voxels on a 64×64×8 grid, 6 classes), which undercuts claims about fine near-field contact geometry.

No statistical rigor: no error bars, no multiple seeds, no significance tests. Ablation deltas of +0.26 to +0.41 mIoU are of the order of typical run-to-run variance and are nonetheless presented as evidence that each component is necessary.

Efficiency and robotics-readiness claims are speculative. '>10 FPS on Jetson Thor' is extrapolated from published tensor budgets rather than measured, no deployment on an actual legged robot is reported, and onboard latency/energy under gait-induced motion is unverified. The limitation section concedes dependence on accurate calibration, which is precisely what a bouncing platform stresses.

Selective framing of the lighting study: in Table 5, at night OneOcc is worse than MonoScene in mIoU (13.50 vs 14.20), yet the text highlights higher precision instead of acknowledging the regression, weakening confidence in the reported robustness story.

Several method details are under-specified, limiting reproducibility: how the cross-grid indices Jℓ are constructed, how channel alignment across scales and projections is performed, and how 'valid voxels (from lifting visibility)' are determined are all left vague.

strengths: Addresses a novel and underexplored setting: monocular panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots, which introduces real challenges (gait-induced jitter, 360-degree continuity, tight compute budgets) that differ meaningfully from autonomous-driving SSC benchmarks.

Introduces two new benchmarks (QuadOcc, a real quadruped first-person 360-degree dataset with time-synced LiDAR and PAL camera; Human360Occ, a CARLA-based human-ego dataset with weather/lighting randomization) and documents their construction pipelines in detail (open-vocabulary segmentation with Grounded-SAM, LiDAR-image label transfer, semantic-guided dynamic mapping, spatiotemporal aggregation).

Coherent set of technical components with clear motivation: Dual-Projection fusion (DP-ER) to retain both raw annular and equirectangular cues; Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) combining Cartesian and cylindrical grids; Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) as a plug-and-play, zero-initialized 2D displacement head; and a depthwise-separable AMoE-3D decoder with dual-path volumetric saliency gating.

Extensive and honestly presented ablations: GDC, DP-ER, BGV, AMoE-3D, number of experts K, field-of-view scaling (90-360 degrees), projection-path (ER vs Raw vs Dual), voxel-resolution scaling, calibration robustness, temporal aggregation, and range-binned safety analysis.

Consistent performance gains across both benchmarks and lighting conditions, outperforming strong vision baselines (MonoScene, SGN, VoxFormer) and rivaling LiDAR-based methods on QuadOcc (20.56 vs LMSCNet 18.44 mIoU), with larger margins under cross-city distribution shift on H3O.

Practical efficiency analysis on a Jetson AGX Orin with INT8/FP16 mixed precision, showing lower latency (~1.34x speedup) and ~30% fewer parameters than MonoScene on H3O, which substantiates the lightweight deployment claim.
Reproducibility effort: detailed per-baseline implementation protocols, dataset deliverable descriptions, sample JSON schemas, and a commitment to release datasets and code.
Thoughtful failure-case and limitations analysis (semantic vs geometric errors, vegetation/rain/dusk cases, sim-to-real gap, single-frame design).
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely on newly introduced benchmarks, so absolute numbers cannot be directly compared to established SSC literature (SemanticKITTI, nuScenes, OpenOcc). Reviewers cannot fully assess the fidelity/difficulty of the semi-automatic QuadOcc ground truth or the simulated H3O labels.

Gains on the real QuadOcc dataset are modest in absolute terms (+1.37 mIoU over MonoScene, +2.12 mIoU over LMSCNet), and the LiDAR-based LMSCNet is trained only on real LiDAR without panoramic-aware adaptations, raising some fairness questions about the baseline comparison despite documented protocols.

The Dual-Projection variant that gives the best accuracy on QuadOcc increases parameters by ~86.5% and peak memory by ~25% while reducing throughput by ~15%; the accuracy-cost trade-off is only partially characterized against the deployment requirements of legged robots.

The voxel-resolution ablation shows that finer 128x128x16 grids yield lower mIoU, which is explained via class imbalance and boundary sensitivity but is an unusual outcome that warrants deeper investigation rather than an efficiency argument.

GDC is modeled as a zero-initialized 2D per-scale displacement, which assumes predominantly vertical gait-induced jitter; it may not account for rotational or combined roll/pitch artifacts or gait effects during sharp turns.
The real benchmark QuadOcc uses only a 6-class taxonomy, which may limit its transferability to richer downstream tasks (manipulation, fine-grained navigation) that legged robots need.
H3O ground truth is simulated (CARLA) with a synthesized vertical bob; the paper itself acknowledges the sim-to-real gap, so generalization to real humanoid platforms is not empirically demonstrated.

Some qualitative figures (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. 6) and the qualitative analysis in Sec. 13 are lengthy but risk being placed in the supplementary material; the main text could better highlight the core distinctiveness of OneOcc.

Dependence on accurate offline PAL calibration (Taylor/OCam) is acknowledged but the sensitivity to realistic calibration drift in legged deployments is only tested synthetically, not on real drift scenarios.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: panoramic semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots, where gait-induced body jitter and 360-degree continuity are critical, unlike most SSC work focused on wheeled platforms and forward-facing sensors.

The proposed OneOcc system is coherent and technically well-motivated: Dual-Projection fusion DP-ER fuses raw annulus and equirectangular views, Bi-Grid Voxelization BGV combines Cartesian and cylindrical spaces, Gait Displacement Compensation GDC corrects jitter before lifting, and Hierarchical AMoE-3D improves anisotropic multi-scale fusion.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two benchmarks QuadOcc and Human360Occ, comparisons with LiDAR-based and vision-based SSC baselines, ablations for each component, FoV and resolution scaling, calibration robustness, temporal aggregation, efficiency on RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin, and qualitative failure-case analysis.

The results support the claims: OneOcc achieves 20.56 mIoU on QuadOcc and 37.29/32.23 mIoU on H3O within/cross-city, outperforming MonoScene and LMSCNet baselines in the reported settings, with larger cross-city gains (+8.08 mIoU) suggesting improved distribution robustness.

The paper contributes two datasets: QuadOcc, a real-world quadruped 360-degree semantic occupancy dataset, and Human360Occ (H3O), a CARLA-based humanoid benchmark with standardized within-/cross-city splits. These are likely useful to the robotics and embodied vision communities.

Reproducibility is generally strong: dataset construction pipelines, calibration, voxelization, label transfer, temporal aggregation, baseline adaptation details, hyperparameters, and planned code/data release are extensively documented.

Efficiency and deployment relevance are addressed: 14.3 FPS with 101.76M parameters on RTX 4090, 13.64 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, and lower parameter count than MonoScene when the raw branch is disabled, showing practical embedded potential.

Ablations are informative and support component choices: GDC, DP-ER, BGV, and AMoE-3D each improve mIoU, and analyses of grid resolution, projection path, FoV, and temporal aggregation provide nuanced design insights.
weaknesses: The method is single-frame and does not perform temporal fusion in the main setting. Dynamic objects are treated as static per frame, and gait compensation only corrects per-frame displacement. The reported temporal-aggregation variants rely on ground-truth pose or add substantial latency/memory, so the default model cannot fully exploit temporal evidence in dynamic legged environments.

The approach assumes accurate intrinsic and extrinsic calibration. Robustness is tested only via synthetic calibration-noise injection, not real sensor drift, online calibration, or long-term extrinsic changes, which are important for field-deployed legged robots.

The datasets have limited scale and diversity: QuadOcc contains 10 scenes and 24K frames in campus-like environments, while Human360Occ is simulated and inherits a sim-to-real gap. Generalization to indoor spaces, dense crowds, off-road terrain, and diverse robot morphologies remains unproven. Ground truth is semi-automatic with LiDAR-image transfer and human verification, but label-noise quantification is limited.

Performance gains over strong baselines are moderate on QuadOcc: +1.37 mIoU over MonoScene and +2.12 over LMSCNet, while the LiDAR-based SGN† reaches 19.72 mIoU, close to OneOcc's 20.56. The margin is not overwhelming and may be sensitive to adaptation choices, although H3O cross-city gains are larger.

The paper does not compare against recent panoramic-specific SSC methods such as OmniOcc or CylinderOcc-style approaches, likely due to unavailable code or different settings. This limits assessment of how OneOcc ranks among specialized panoramic occupancy pipelines.

Several technical components are incremental or combine existing ideas: dual projection, cylindrical/Cartesian voxelization, mixture-of-experts decoding, and zero-initialized displacement heads. Individual gains are small in ablations (e.g., +0.39 mIoU for GDC, +0.26 for AMoE-3D), and the overall novelty is more in the integrated system and benchmarks than in a single fundamentally new mechanism.

The evaluation measures semantic occupancy quality (IoU/mIoU) but does not include downstream navigation, traversability, footstep planning, or closed-loop robot deployment. The practical benefit for legged robots is therefore inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

The main paper is dense with many components, equations, and design choices; some details are relegated to extensive supplementary material. While the writing is organized, the core method may be hard to fully assess without the supplementary sections.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored setting: panoramic single-camera semantic scene completion for legged/humanoid robots, with practical constraints such as 360° continuity, gait-induced jitter, and onboard compute.

Introduces two benchmarks, QuadOcc (real quadruped) and Human360Occ (CARLA human-ego), with day/dusk/night, weather diversity, and within-/cross-city splits; these could be useful community resources if released and properly validated.

Provides a broad empirical study: multiple baselines, ablations over core modules, lighting, field-of-view, voxel resolution, calibration robustness, temporal aggregation, qualitative comparisons, and edge-device runtime/memory analysis.

The proposed pipeline is sensible and deployable in principle: dual-projection encoders, bi-grid voxelization, gait displacement compensation, hierarchical AMoE-3D, and lightweight 3D decoding are integrated into a single-camera framework.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited and incremental. The individual components—dual projection, cylindrical/Cartesian voxelization, mixture-of-experts fusion, and displacement compensation—are largely derived from existing ideas, and the ablation gains are small: on QuadOcc, GDC adds +0.39 mIoU, DP-ER +0.41, BGV +0.41, and AMoE-3D +0.26 (Table 4). This does not provide strong evidence that the specific combination is necessary or substantially better.

The Gait Displacement Compensation module is conceptually and technically questionable. It regresses a global 2D displacement per scale via GAP+Linear and applies the same offset to all voxel queries; this cannot capture spatially varying, depth-dependent, or per-pixel motion blur. Since the model is single-frame and has no temporal/IMU reference, it is unclear how it estimates “gait phase” rather than a dataset-specific bias. Figure 8 is only qualitative and lacks ground-truth displacement or motion-blur validation.

Benchmark fairness and evaluation are concerning. The paper introduces its own benchmarks and retrains baselines with modified voxel grids, classes, input modalities, and losses. LiDAR baselines are adapted to the authors’ small 64×64×8 volumes, and the vision baselines may not be fully tuned under the same resource constraints. Claims such as surpassing LiDAR baselines are therefore not well supported as generalizable comparisons.

The Human360Occ dataset is simulated in CARLA with a simplistic speed-conditioned vertical bob, not real humanoid or legged gait. QuadOcc is semi-automatically labeled with LiDAR-SLAM, Grounded-SAM, and manual fixes, but the paper provides no independent validation of ground-truth quality. The “legged/humanoid” claim is stronger than the evidence, since no real humanoid platform is evaluated.

The main operating resolution is coarse (64×64×8 at 0.4 m), which limits relevance for humanoid manipulation, fine-grained contact reasoning, and small obstacles. Rare classes such as pedestrian and vehicle achieve very low IoU/mIoU, and the paper itself shows that higher resolution (128×128×16) hurts aggregate mIoU and is much slower/heavier. The practical impact of the method is therefore constrained.

Reproducibility is currently limited: datasets and code are only promised, and the construction pipeline depends on multiple external models/tools (Grounded-SAM, LiDAR-SLAM, CARLA, OCam/Taylor calibration, custom labeling). The paper does not establish that the ground truth or calibration pipeline is robust enough for others to reproduce or trust.

The presentation is overloaded with supplementary-style details, while the main paper sometimes overstates conclusions (“sets a new state of the art,” “rivals or surpasses classical LiDAR baselines”) relative to the evidence from self-defined benchmarks and narrow ablations. The contribution would be clearer with tighter claims and stronger validation.
